sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-18. 'Line charts display continuous data as points connected by lines, making them ideal for visualizing trends over time'; a field in the Legend well makes one line per value; small multiples give one chart per category; a continuous X-axis plots dates proportionally. That summing a per-store rate column does not give a region's rate (a ratio of sums does) is arithmetic, stated as the author's.

brief.situation: You own the Operations report at Harbor & Pine Furniture (fictional). The Returns page has one visual: a pie chart of ReturnRate by Region. The head of operations asks whether the return rate is rising month over month and where. The ops review is at 11:00. It is 10:05.
handover: ReturnRate is a column on the Stores table: each store's return rate for the last 12 months, a percentage.
Returns[Units] and Sales[Units] are by date and store; the Date table is marked as a date table.
howItWorks: Pick a step from the action list: look, change, check or ship. Nothing you pick is typed or executed: every step shows an authored result.
Each step takes working minutes, and the clock moves by the minutes it takes. The deadline runs on the same clock.
Shipping is final for this case. Afterwards you record what you found and explain your reasoning.

scoring.modelReasoning: The question is a trend over time by region, so the visual needs months on the X-axis and one series per region: a line chart. The value must be a rate, so compute returned units divided by sold units as a measure instead of adding store percentages. Check the October values against the returns sheet. A pie shows composition at one moment; clustered columns are right but hard to read for a trend; a line of summed rates shows numbers over 400%.
